Since 11:04 UTC no job could get a runner. Every provisioning attempt died at:

```

Chain of evidence:
1. Host clock was fine (chrony synced, RTC correct).

4. Constant countdown across retries confirmed it: the skew never shrank, because every fork restarted from the same stale epoch.

apt refuses an index whose `Date` is in the guest's future, so `apt-get update` exited 100, provisioning failed, orchestrator retried every ~28s forever.

Restarting the service forced a fresh golden bake; `apt-get update` in it now exits 0.

## Latent bug worth filing
Nothing resyncs guest wall clock on fork/thaw — the fork base's clock is frozen at bake time and inherited by every runner. The skew equals how long the golden has sat frozen, so this recurs whenever a golden survives a few hours without a fingerprint change (exactly what happened after this morning's reboot: golden baked 11:04, still in use at 16:04). Options, cheapest first: have the agent set time from the host on thaw/exec, run `hwclock -s`/chrony at fork start, or refuse a fork base older than N minutes.

# 1. smolvm bug: forked clones inherit the golden's wall clock, forever

**Repo:** `/Users/bnjoroge/smolvm` (deployed build: smolvm 1.8.3)

## Statement

A CoW fork restores the golden's guest memory, which includes the guest's `CLOCK_REALTIME` state. Nothing re-seeds it in the clone. So every clone's wall clock equals **the instant the forkpoint was created, plus the clone's own uptime** — i.e. the clone is behind real time by the *wall-clock age of the forkpoint*, and it never catches up.

## Reproduction (no preloop needed)

```sh
smolvm machine start --name golden --forkable --image ubuntu:24.04
# let it reach its forkpoint, then age the forkpoint deliberately:
sleep 900

smolvm machine fork --golden golden --name clone1
smolvm machine exec --name clone1 -- sh -c 'date -u; cut -d. -f1 /proc/uptime'
date -u    # host
```

**Expected:** clone within ~1s of host.
**Actual:** clone is ~15 min behind, and the identity holds exactly:

```
guest_now == forkpoint_creation_time + clone_uptime
```

Increase `sleep` and the skew grows 1:1. The clone never self-corrects — verified against a clone with **652 s uptime**, still 3 m 27 s behind (well past the 60 s timesync interval).

### Production measurement backing this

| | |
|---|---|
| `golden fork base ready` logged at | `16:19:52` |
| clone `preloop-runner-0-2` guest clock | `16:30:44` |
| clone uptime | `652 s` |
| $16{:}30{:}44 - 652\,\text{s}$ | $= 16{:}19{:}52$ — exactly the forkpoint |
| host at time of reading | `16:34:11` (skew $3\,\text{m}\,27\,\text{s}$) |

Earlier the same day, a golden baked at `11:04:12` was still the fork base at `16:04` → every clone booted **5 h** behind, which broke apt in all of them:

```
E: Release file for .../noble-updates/InRelease is not valid yet
   (invalid for another 2h 14min 26s)
```

The countdown was byte-identical across 214 consecutive attempts — the tell that the base epoch is fixed, not drifting.

## Why the two existing safety nets both miss

**`crates/smolvm-agent/src/main.rs:180-201` — `maybe_set_clock_from_host()`**

```rust
const Y2020_SECS: i64 = 1_577_836_800;
...
if now_secs >= Y2020_SECS { return; }   // ← bails here
```

Designed for WHP guests booting at ~1999. A clone inherits a clock that is stale but plainly post-2020, so the guard returns early. Also irrelevant in the clone regardless: `main()` never re-runs — the restored guest resumes *past* it.

**`crates/smolvm-agent/src/timesync.rs` + `main.rs:246` — `timesync::spawn()`**

Receives host `CLOCK_REALTIME` pushes on vsock DGRAM port 123. Its own header scopes it: *"On hypervisors without a guest-readable paravirt clock (macOS/HVF and Windows/WHP), libkrun's host-side `TimesyncThread` pushes…"*. On the Linux/KVM host there is no such push — empirically proven by the 652 s-uptime clone still being 3 m 27 s off, when the documented interval is 60 s. The fallback that saves macOS sleep (issue #521) simply does not fire here.

## Fix site

`src/agent/fork.rs::build_rejuvenation_script` (~lines 959–1020) already exists precisely to scrub state that goes stale on a fork. It rejuvenates hostname, `machine-id`, dbus id, SSH host keys, cloud-init instance state, and the RNG seed — **but not the clock**, which is the same class of inherited-stale state.

The script is host-generated and already interpolates host-side values (`{s}` = seed), and runs as root in the guest, so the minimal fix is one interpolated statement:

```sh
date -s @{host_epoch_at_fork} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true;
```

Alternatives, in order of increasing scope: have the guest agent re-seed on seeing `RESTORED_PATH`; or run libkrun's `TimesyncThread` on Linux/KVM too, which would also bound drift for long-lived clones.

## Blast radius beyond apt

Any signed/time-bounded material inside a clone: TLS `notBefore` validation, JWT/OIDC `iat`/`exp`, registration-token expiry against the control plane, and every job log/artifact timestamp.

## Note for preloop's side of this

Goldens are keyed by content fingerprint only, with no age bound — `crates/preloop-orchestrator/src/environment.rs:372` says it outright: *"the pool silently keeps the old golden forever"*. So on any server that runs for hours without a fingerprint change, the skew grows until apt breaks. **This will recur on `main`.** Until smolvm is fixed, the durable mitigation is a golden TTL (re-bake when the fork base exceeds ~1 h) rather than a manual `systemctl restart preloop`.

---

# 2. The GitHub App genuinely isn't subscribed — and one warning entry is a preloop bug

I minted an app JWT on `main` with the deployed PEM and asked GitHub directly:

```
app_id=4429171   slug=aksh-dogfood-app
events:      ["pull_request","push"]
permissions: {"checks":"write","contents":"read","metadata":"read","pull_requests":"read"}
hook url:    https://aksh.preloop.dev/api/v1/github/webhooks
```

So preloop's warning is reporting GitHub's own answer accurately (`github_app.rs::read_app_events_at` just reads `GET /app` → `.events`). Two separate things are going on.

## a) Why your ticks didn't take: permission gating

GitHub only renders an event checkbox if the app holds the permission that event belongs to. With the four permissions above:

| Event | Needs | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `issues`, `issue_comment` | **Issues** | permission absent → checkbox never appears |
| `workflow_run` | **Actions** | permission absent → checkbox never appears |
| `check_run`, `check_suite` | Checks ✓ | allowed, but unticked |
| `create`, `delete`, `release`, `repository_dispatch`, `workflow_dispatch` | Contents ✓ | allowed, but unticked |
| `pull_request_review` | Pull requests ✓ | allowed, but unticked |

So the fix is two steps, in order: **add the Issues and Actions permissions first**, save, then the missing checkboxes appear and can be ticked. Permission additions also have to be **accepted for the installation** (GitHub emails an approval / shows it under the install's settings) before those events actually flow.

For the second group — allowed by current permissions yet still unticked — the likely causes are editing a different app or the page not being saved. Worth confirming you were on **`aksh-dogfood-app` (id 4429171)**, since that's the one this server authenticates as. Permission→event mapping above is from GitHub's docs, so double-check it against the UI as you go. `[INFERENCE]`

## b) `pull_request_target` is a preloop bug — that one can never be satisfied

`crates/preloop-runner-server/src/github_app.rs::required_trigger_events()` lists `pull_request_target`. That is **not a webhook event** — it's a workflow `on:` trigger, fed by the ordinary `pull_request` delivery. GitHub's webhook events reference contains **0** occurrences of it (against 18 for `pull_request_review`, 9 for `workflow_run`).

Consequence: even after you tick every real event, `/app` can never return `pull_request_target`, so `warn_missing_trigger_events` fires on every startup forever — alarm fatigue on a warning that's supposed to mean something. It should be dropped from the list (its coverage is implied by `pull_request`).

## Impact right now

Low for core CI: push/PR checks work, which is why runs are executing. The missing events only disable the extra triggers (`workflow_dispatch`, `issue_comment` commands, `check_run` re-runs, `release`, etc.).

---

## Current state of `main`

Service active, API 200, golden re-baked at 16:19:52, runners `-0-1`/`-0-2`/`-0-3` registering and executing job steps, **0** provisioning failures since the restart (against 214 in the previous 6 h). The clock skew is already back to ~3.5 min and climbing at 1:1 with wall time — it becomes fatal again once it exceeds the age of Ubuntu's published index, so the golden TTL is the thing worth doing before tomorrow.

what the app may READ] --> B[Gate 2: Event subscriptions
which events GitHub SENDS] B --> C[Webhook delivered to preloop] ``` **Gate 1 — Permissions.** Your app has four: Checks (write), Contents (read), Metadata (read), Pull requests (read). **Gate 2 — "Subscribe to events" checkboxes.** GitHub only *renders a checkbox* for an event whose permission you already hold. Neither, actually — you're mixing up two separate things that share the name. ## The checkbox is in the App's own settings, not in your repo It lives in exactly one place, global to the app — not per-PR, not in the Actions tab: ``` https://github.com/settings/apps/aksh-dogfood-app/permissions ``` That page is titled **"Permissions & events"**. Scroll past the permissions to the **"Subscribe to events"** section at the bottom — it's a flat list of checkboxes (`Check run`, `Create`, `Delete`, `Issues`, `Release`, `Workflow dispatch`, …). Tick `Workflow dispatch`, hit **Save changes**. It applies to the whole app across every repo it's installed on. Your repo's UI never shows it. ## The Actions-tab thing is a different mechanism The **"Run workflow" button** in the Actions tab is per-workflow, and appears when a workflow file declares `on: workflow_dispatch` (and the file exists on the **default branch** — a common gotcha, since it won't show up for a workflow that only exists on a feature branch). So the two connect like this: ```mermaid graph LR A["Run workflow button
(Actions tab)
or POST dispatch API"] -->|emits| B[workflow_dispatch event] B --> C{App subscribed?} C -->|checkbox ticked| D[Delivered to preloop] C -->|not ticked| E[Dropped, never sent] ``` The button **emits**; the App checkbox decides whether preloop **hears about it**. Two different surfaces, both needed for that path to work end-to-end. Good news on this one: `workflow_dispatch` only requires the Contents permission (docs [4], confirmed above), and your app already has `contents: read`. So unlike `issues`/`workflow_run`, that checkbox is already visible on the page right now — it's simply unticked. ## You may not need any of this If your goal is just "manually kick off a run in preloop," the webhook path is a detour. The deployed binary already does it directly: ``` --event Simulate a trigger event (push, pull_request, merge_group, …) ``` So `preloop run --event workflow_dispatch` runs a dispatch-only workflow locally with no GitHub round-trip, no checkbox, no permission change. The webhook subscription only matters if you specifically want *clicking the button on github.com* to drive a preloop run.

That's the one — the webhook warning. Here's exactly what's wrong with it.

## The bug

`crates/preloop-runner-server/src/github_app.rs:1338` — `required_trigger_events()` lists 14 events that preloop compares against what `GET /app` reports. Three of those entries can **never** appear in that response, so the warning can never go quiet:

- **`pull_request_target`** — not a webhook event at all. It's a workflow `on:` trigger, fed by the ordinary `pull_request` delivery. GitHub has no such event to report, so this line is permanently unsatisfiable.
- **`check_run` and `check_suite`** — auto-subscribed for any app with `checks: write` (GitHub docs: *"GitHub Apps with write-level access for the 'Checks' permission are automatically subscribed to this webhook event"*). They're delivered but never listed in `.events`. Your app proves it: 17 `check_suite` deliveries while `.events` says only `["pull_request","push"]`.

## Why it matters

The warning fires from three call sites — `bootstrap.rs:499`, `bootstrap.rs:520` (every startup), and `github_app.rs:1317` (after every webhook-config update). So a **perfectly configured app still gets warned at every boot**, forever. That's a diagnostic that cries wolf, and operators learn to scroll past it — which defeats the point of writing it in the first place.

It also actively misled us today: it told you to go tick `check_suite`, which was already working fine.

## Why the test didn't catch it

`github_app.rs:2222`:

```rust
let complete = required_trigger_events()
    .iter()
    .map(|event| (*event).to_owned())
    .collect::<Vec<_>>();
assert!(missing_trigger_events(&complete).is_empty(), …);
```

It builds the "complete subscription" *from the list under test*. Tautology — it verifies internal consistency and passes no matter how many fictional event names the list contains.

## Fix shape

1. Drop `pull_request_target` (its coverage is implied by `pull_request`).
2. Make `check_run`/`check_suite` conditional on the Checks permission. `read_app_events_at` already fetches the `GET /app` body that carries `.permissions` — it just discards everything but `.events`, so this is widening one return type, not a new API call.
3. Report the **required permission** next to each genuinely-missing event (`issues` → Issues, `workflow_run` → Actions). Right now the message says "tick the missing events" for events whose checkbox GitHub doesn't render — which is precisely the dead end you hit.
4. Replace the tautological test with a hardcoded literal of real event names, so a fictional entry fails CI.

That's independent of the other bug from earlier — the smolvm fork clock skew plus the missing golden TTL, which is the one that actually took CI down for five hours.

+        event("workflow_dispatch", "contents"),
+        event("workflow_run", "actions"),
+        event("repository_dispatch", "contents"),
+        event("issue_comment", "issues"),
+        event("issues", "issues"),
+        implicit("check_run", "checks"),
+        implicit("check_suite", "checks"),
+        event("create", "contents"),
+        event("delete", "contents"),
+        event("release", "contents"),
+    ]
+}
+
+/// A required event GitHub does not currently deliver to preloop.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub(crate) struct MissingTriggerEvent {
+    pub event: &'static str,
+    pub permission: &'static str,
+    /// Whether the App already holds the gating permission — i.e. whether the
+    /// operator can tick the checkbox today or must widen permissions first.
+    pub permission_granted: bool,
+}
+
+/// The required trigger events `subscription` does not cover, in canonical order.
+pub(crate) fn missing_trigger_events(subscription: &AppSubscription) -> Vec<MissingTriggerEvent> {
+    required_trigger_events()
+        .iter()
+        .filter(|required| !subscription.delivers(required))
+        .map(|required| MissingTriggerEvent {
+            event: required.event,
+            permission: required.permission,
+            permission_granted: subscription.has_permission(required.permission),
+        })
+        .collect()
+}
+
+/// Loudly warn when an App's subscription does not cover the trigger set.
+///
+/// GitHub cannot change an App's event subscription through the API — only the
+/// App settings UI can — so this is a warning with exact instructions, not an
+/// attempt to fix the App. Events whose permission is missing are reported
+/// separately: their checkbox does not exist until the permission is granted
+/// and the installation accepts the change.
+pub(crate) fn warn_missing_trigger_events(app_id: &str, subscription: &AppSubscription) {
+    let missing = missing_trigger_events(subscription);
+    if missing.is_empty() {
+        return;
+    }
+    let all = missing
+        .iter()
+        .map(|missing| missing.event)
+        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
+        .join(", ");
+    let tickable = missing
+        .iter()
+        .filter(|missing| missing.permission_granted)
+        .map(|missing| missing.event)
+        .collect::<Vec<_>>();
+    let mut blocked: BTreeMap<&str, Vec<&str>> = BTreeMap::new();
+    for missing in missing.iter().filter(|missing| !missing.permission_granted) {
+        blocked.entry(missing.permission).or_default().push(missing.event);
+    }
+    let mut steps = Vec::new();
+    if !tickable.is_empty() {
+        steps.push(format!(
+            "tick these under Subscribe to events: {}",
+            tickable.join(", ")
+        ));
+    }
+    if !blocked.is_empty() {
+        let grants = blocked
+            .iter()
+            .map(|(permission, events)| format!("{permission} (for {})", events.join(", ")))
+            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
+            .join("; ");
+        steps.push(format!(
+            "grant these permissions first — GitHub hides an event's checkbox \
+             until its permission is granted, and the installation must accept \
+             the change before delivery starts: {grants}"
+        ));
+    }
+    tracing::warn!(
+        app_id,
+        missing = %all,
+        "GitHub App {app_id} does not receive webhook events preloop needs \
+         (missing: {all}). GitHub will never deliver those events to preloop. \
+         Open https://github.com/settings/apps/{app_id}/permissions and {}.",
+        steps.join(", then ")
+    );
+}
*** End Patch

import subprocess
msg = """fix(github-app): stop warning about undeliverable webhook events

The startup subscription check warned forever on a correctly configured
App, because `required_trigger_events()` listed three events `GET /app`
can never report:

- `pull_request_target` is not a webhook event at all. It is a workflow
  trigger preloop synthesizes from the `pull_request` webhook
  (`events/pull_request.rs`), so GitHub has nothing to report and the
  entry could never be satisfied.
- `check_run`/`check_suite` are auto-subscribed for Apps holding
  `checks: write` and are omitted from `events`, so their absence never
  meant they were undelivered. Verified against a live App: 17
  `check_suite` deliveries while `events` was `["pull_request","push"]`.

The warning also told operators to "tick the missing events" for events
whose checkbox GitHub does not render, because the App lacks the gating
permission -- a dead end. It now reads permissions from the same
`GET /app` response and splits its advice: events tickable today, versus
events needing a permission grant (and installation acceptance) first.

`read_app_events_at` becomes `read_app_subscription_at`, returning events
plus permissions as `AppSubscription`; the per-event permission mapping
mirrors each event's "must have at least read-level access for the ..."
clause in GitHub's webhook events reference.

The old test built its "complete subscription" from the table under
test, so it passed for fictional event names. It now asserts every entry
against a literal list of real GitHub webhook events.

Drive-by, unrelated: fix a `clippy::manual_is_multiple_of` error in
store.rs that already failed `just test-ci` on main under Rust 1.97.

**1. I had to deviate from submit-before-push, and here's why.** The first submission (run #32) failed in `actions/checkout`:

```
git fetch --depth=1 origin +0000000000000000000000000000000000000000:refs/remotes/origin/main
fatal: remote error: upload-pack: not our ref 0000…0000
```

A submitted run carries no commit SHA, so any workflow starting with `actions/checkout` dies before reaching your code. For a checkout-based workflow the commit must be fetchable, so I pushed the branch, then re-submitted (`--event workflow_dispatch`, since `on.push` is restricted to `main`). Worth deciding whether the rule should carve out checkout-based workflows, or whether `submit` should grow a `--sha` and bind the snapshot to the checkout.

**2. Run #34 is still queued, behind the clock bug.** The pool has one free slot and it's busy with another run's `cargo test`. More importantly, the skew I predicted this morning is back and growing on schedule:

| Host time | Guest time in job logs | Skew |
|---|---|---|
| 16:34 | 16:30 | 3.5 min |
| 17:25 | 16:50 | 35 min |
| 17:53 | 17:08 | **44 min** |

It's tracking wall-clock age exactly as the smolvm analysis predicted, and once it passes the age of Ubuntu's published index, `apt` starts failing again and provisioning re-enters the retry loop that took CI down for five hours. content.text:
Correct me being unclear earlier — **I never fixed the clock bug. I reset it.** Different things.

## What I actually did

Restarting preloop forced a fresh golden bake at 16:19:52. A golden baked from a cold boot gets the host's time, so at that instant skew was zero. That's it. I zeroed a counter that immediately starts climbing again — I changed nothing about *why* it climbs.

## Live measurement, 60 seconds ago

```
preloop-runner-0-17   guest=17:13:43   uptime=1590s
preloop-runner-0-18   guest=16:48:18   uptime=65s
host=18:01:35
```

Look at `0-18`. It was **65 seconds old** and already **1h13m behind**. That's the whole bug in one line: it isn't drifting, it's being *born* stale.

Both clones compute the same boot epoch:

$$17{:}13{:}43 - 1590\,\text{s} = 16{:}47{:}13 \qquad 16{:}48{:}18 - 65\,\text{s} = 16{:}47{:}13$$

Identical. Every clone resumes from the forkpoint's frozen memory image, inherits that instant, and counts up from there. Skew = how long ago the forkpoint was taken:

$$18{:}01{:}35 - 16{:}47{:}13 - 65\,\text{s} = 1\text{h}\,13\text{m}\,17\text{s}$$

A restart moves the forkpoint to "now." It does not make clones read the host clock, because nothing in the restore path ever sets the clock — `build_rejuvenation_script` resets hostname, machine-id, dbus id, SSH keys, and the RNG seed, but not time — and on Linux/KVM there's no host→guest timesync push to catch it later (that path is HVF/WHP only, which is why a 652 s-uptime clone was still behind).

So: **~73 minutes now**, growing one second per second, and it re-breaks `apt` once it exceeds the age of Ubuntu's published index. Same outage as this morning, just on a fresh countdown that started at 16:19.

## Three options, different scopes

1. **Restart preloop again** — 30 seconds, resets skew to zero, buys a few hours. Pure stopgap, and it kills the `cargo test` currently running.
2. **Golden TTL in preloop** — re-bake when the fork base exceeds ~1 h. Bounds the damage permanently, ships through the preloop release path you already use. Doesn't fix the bug, but makes it non-fatal.
3. **Fix smolvm** — one interpolated `date -s @<host_epoch_at_fork>` in `build_rejuvenation_script`, where the host already interpolates the RNG seed and the guest exec runs as root. Root cause, correct fix — but it needs a smolvm rebuild and a redeploy of `/opt/smolvm/smolvm-bin` on `main`, since prod runs the prebuilt 1.8.3.

My recommendation is 3 for correctness plus 2 as defense-in-depth, since 3 only reaches prod on a redeploy and 2 protects you regardless of which smolvm build is installed.

Which do you want me to take? I'd start with the smolvm patch (it's small and I've already traced the exact call site), unless you'd rather I land the preloop TTL first since that ships without touching the smolvm deploy.

Your systemd drop-in says one thing, the running process says the opposite:

```
/etc/systemd/system/preloop.service.d/10-smolvm-env.conf   →  PRELOOP_USE_FORK=false
/proc/<preloop>/environ                                    →  PRELOOP_USE_FORK=true

The unit has `EnvironmentFile=/etc/preloop/preloop.env`, and that file wins:

```
/etc/preloop/preloop.env   (mtime 2026-08-20 17:54:43)
  5: PRELOOP_RUNNER_POOL_SIZE=1
  6: PRELOOP_USE_FORK=true

```

Your drop-in's `=false` is dead config. It has never taken effect since the env file was written.

## Timeline

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Aug 19 05:03 | smolvm 1.8.3 installed |
| Aug 20 03:23 | drop-in written with `PRELOOP_USE_FORK=false` |
| Aug 20 17:31 | preloop 0.31.1 deployed |
| **Aug 20 17:54** | **`preloop.env` sets `PRELOOP_USE_FORK=true`** — fork path switched on |
| Aug 28 10:40 | `main` back up after ~5 h down |
| Aug 28 11:04 | golden baked… and never rebaked for 5 h → apt breaks |

Before Aug 20, `use_fork` was off: runners were built per job from the packed artifact — a **cold boot**, which reads the host clock and is therefore always correct. That's the behavior you remember. After Aug 20 every runner became a CoW clone of a frozen golden, which inherits the golden's wall clock.

## Why it took 8 days to bite

With forking on, skew equals the *age of the forkpoint*. Goldens get rebaked whenever the fingerprint changes or the service restarts — and you deploy often, so goldens stayed young and skew stayed under the threshold. apt only fails once skew exceeds the age of Ubuntu's published index (hours). Today was the first long quiet stretch: down ~5 h, back at 10:40, golden baked 11:04, nothing rebaked it, skew crossed the line, 214 provisioning failures.

So: latent since Aug 20, triggered by the first idle period long enough to age a golden.

## This changes the fix menu

There's now a cheaper option than the two I gave you:

0. **Set `PRELOOP_USE_FORK=false` in `/etc/preloop/preloop.env`** (the file that actually wins) — one line, no code, no deploy. Restores exactly the pre-Aug-20 behavior you remember, and eliminates the clock bug by construction, since cold-booted runners never inherit a clock. Cost: you lose fork startup speed — each runner boots from the packed artifact instead of CoW-cloning, so job start gets slower.

That trades against keeping fork (golden TTL, or the smolvm `date -s` patch), which preserves fast starts but keeps the inheritance behavior that needs bounding.

Both confirmed. Here's each. ## 1. "Bounding" = capping the error, not removing it Skew grows linearly with the age of the forkpoint: $$\text{skew}(t) = t - t_{\text{fork}}$$ A TTL says: rebake the golden once it's older than $T$. That doesn't stop clones inheriting a stale clock — it just guarantees the staleness never exceeds $T$: $$\text{skew} \in [0,\ T]$$ Contrast with **eliminating** it, where clones read the host clock and skew ≈ 0 permanently — that's what cold-booting (`PRELOOP_USE_FORK=false`) or a `date -s` at fork does. Bounding is the "keep the fast path, make the error small enough not to matter" option. Whether that works depends entirely on the failure threshold — which brings us to your second question, and it turns out to be bad news for the TTL idea. ## 2. Why Ubuntu specifically apt refuses repository metadata **dated in the future**. It's a deliberate security control: a future-dated index is what a rollback/replay attack looks like, so apt won't touch it. The check compares your clock against the `Date:` field in `InRelease`, with a tolerance of `Acquire::Max-FutureTime` (tiny by default; the escape hatches are `Acquire::Check-Date=false` or raising `Max-FutureTime`). The failure condition is therefore: $$\text{skew} > \text{age of the published index at fetch time}$$ Here's the live index right now: ``` Date: Fri, 28 Aug 2026 13:18:52 UTC now: Fri, 28 Aug 2026 18:10:22 UTC index age: 4.86 hours ``` That reconciles this morning's error exactly. The message said *"invalid for another 2h 14min"* at a 5 h skew, which puts the index age at that moment at 2 h 46 m: $$5\text{h} - 2\text{h}46\text{m} = 2\text{h}14\text{m} \quad\checkmark$$ **Why apt and not something else:** it has by far the tightest freshness window in the bake. TLS certificates are valid for months or years, so an hour of skew doesn't scratch them. Git doesn't care about time at all. apt is the only step whose validity window is measured in hours — and the bake runs it early, so it's the first tripwire. (JWTs are the other short-window credential, minutes-scale — those would break next, which is why I flagged registration tokens as blast radius.) ## The part that changes my earlier advice That index age is not a fixed threshold — it's a sawtooth. Ubuntu republishes `noble-updates` periodically; at each publish the age resets to ~0 and then climbs. So your tolerance oscillates between roughly zero and the publish interval: ```mermaid graph LR A["index published
age = 0
tolerance ≈ 0"] --> B["age climbs
tolerance grows"] B --> C["next publish
tolerance resets to ≈ 0"] C --> B ``` The consequence: **right after a publish, essentially any skew fails.** A guest 30 minutes behind, fetching a 5-minute-old index, sees a future date and refuses it. So a TTL would have to keep skew down to a few minutes to be genuinely safe — and a bake takes ~9 minutes. Rebaking every ~15 minutes to dodge this is absurd. I was too generous to option 2 earlier: **the TTL doesn't actually bound the problem to a safe level; it just makes failures rarer and random.** You'd be trading a reproducible outage for an intermittent one, which is worse to debug. That leaves the two real fixes: - **`PRELOOP_USE_FORK=false`** in `/etc/preloop/preloop.env` — cold-booted runners, skew structurally impossible, exactly the pre-Aug-20 behavior. Costs fork startup speed. - **The smolvm `date -s` at fork** — keeps fork speed, fixes the root cause, needs a smolvm rebuild and redeploy. A TTL is still worth having as a backstop for *other* age-related staleness, but it shouldn't be the answer to this.
wait im confused. so when we fork, isnthe skew the difference ebtween the golden at snapshot time and the current at ths host?

Yes — with one refinement that's worth getting exact, because it explains something you'd otherwise find weird.

## The formula

The skew is fixed **at the moment each clone is born**, and equals the forkpoint's age *at that moment*:

$$\text{skew} = B - F$$

where $F$ is the snapshot instant and $B$ is when that clone was created.

Derivation: the clone's clock resumes at $F$ and then ticks normally at 1 s/s, so at host time $H$ it reads $F + U$ where $U$ is the clone's uptime. Therefore

$$\text{skew} = H - (F + U) = H - F - (H - B) = B - F$$

The $H$ cancels. So while a clone runs, **its skew doesn't grow** — its clock ticks at the same rate as the host's. What grows is the skew of each *newly created* clone, because $F$ stays pinned while $B$ marches on.

## Confirmed against the live measurements

Both clones inherited the same forkpoint, $F = 16{:}47{:}13$:

| clone | uptime | guest clock | born at $B$ | skew $= B - F$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0-17` | 1590 s | 17:13:43 | 17:35:05 | **47 m 52 s** |
| `0-18` | 65 s | 16:48:18 | 18:00:30 | **1 h 13 m 17 s** |

Host was 18:01:35 for both readings. Two VMs alive at the same instant, same golden, **different skews** — because `0-18` was born 25 minutes later than `0-17`, off the same frozen snapshot.

That's the part that trips people up: it isn't one global drift number. Every clone carries its own fixed offset, and **the newest clone is always the worst one**.

## Why that matters for the failure

apt runs inside a clone, so the number that gets compared against the index date is that clone's birth-time skew — i.e. how old the golden was when that particular runner was created. The longer a golden survives, the more broken each successive runner is, while the ones already running are unaffected.

Which is exactly the shape of this morning's outage: the golden sat at $F = 11{:}04$, and by 16:04 every *newly minted* runner was born 5 h behind and failed apt immediately, retry after retry, each new clone as bad as the last.

msg = """fix(fork): re-stamp a clone's wall clock to host time at fork

A CoW fork restores the golden's guest RAM, which carries the golden's
CLOCK_REALTIME frozen at forkpoint-bake time. On Linux/KVM nothing
re-seeds it: the boot-time seeder ran only in the golden's now-past

  "body": "## Problem

A CoW fork restores the golden's guest RAM, which carries the golden's `CLOCK_REALTIME` frozen at forkpoint-bake time. On Linux/KVM nothing re-seeds it — the boot-time seeder ran only in the golden's now-past `main()`, and libkrun pushes timesync on HVF/WHP only. Every clone therefore reads `forkpoint_bake + clone_uptime` and stays that far behind real time for its whole life.

The skew is fixed at each clone's birth and equals the forkpoint's age at that moment, so it grows without bound while a golden stays in service. Two clones alive at once, same golden, measured in preloop production:

| clone | uptime | guest clock | skew |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0-17` | 1590 s | 17:13:43 | 47 m 52 s |
| `0-18` | 65 s | 16:48:18 | **1 h 13 m 17 s** |

Host was 18:01:35 for both. A clone 65 seconds old was already 73 minutes behind — it is not drift, clones are *born* stale.

Downstream, apt refuses future-dated repository metadata (rollback protection), so once skew exceeds the published index age every clone fails:

```
E: Release file for .../noble-updates/InRelease is not valid yet
   (invalid for another 2h 14min 26s)
```

A golden left in service ~5 h produced 214 consecutive failed runner provisions and took preloop CI down.

## Fix

Re-stamp the wall clock in the rejuvenation script, which already exists to scrub state a clone must not inherit (machine-id, SSH host keys, dbus id, cloud-init state, RNG seed). The wall clock is the same class of inherited-stale state and was simply missing from that list. kvmclock keeps the *rate* correct, so a one-shot offset fix is sufficient — no continuous pusher needed.

Unlike the identity scrub, this step is deliberately **fail-soft**: a skewed clock is recoverable and is not an impersonation vector, so it must not abort `set -e` and tear the clone down. It stays observable via a `rejuvenate-stage=clock-failed` marker rather than a silent `|| true`, so a failure is diagnosable instead of reproducing the very silent-skew bug this fixes.

The host epoch is captured after the agent-connect backoff and the script is rebuilt on every attempt, so retries cannot apply a stale epoch. Non-Linux hosts pass `0` and skip the step — libkrun's time-sync pusher already owns `CLOCK_REALTIME` there and must not be fought by a second clock source. A zero epoch skips rather than setting the guest to 1970, which would be worse than a stale-but-plausible clock.

## Tests

`rejuvenation_script_restamps_the_wall_clock` covers the re-stamp, the fail-soft marker, ordering before identity writes, and the zero-epoch skip. `rejuvenation_clock_reset_is_limited_to_linux_kvm_hosts` and `clock_reset_failure_marker_is_detected_on_successful_exec` cover host gating and marker detection. All 23 `agent::fork` tests pass.

Host epoch is captured after the agent-connect backoff and the script is rebuilt per attempt, so retries cannot apply a stale epoch. Non-Linux hosts pass `0` and skip: libkrun's time-sync pusher already owns `CLOCK_REALTIME` there.

## What each one is

**`zizmor / GitHub Actions Security Analysis with zizmor (push)` — Successful in 9s**
That's **GitHub's own hosted Actions**, running `.github/workflows/zizmor.yml` on their runners. The UI format is `<workflow name> / <job name> (<event>)`, so "zizmor" is the workflow's `name:` and "GitHub Actions Security Analysis with zizmor" is the job's `name:`. 9 seconds because it's a tiny lint on a warm hosted runner.

**`zizmor` — Queued, waiting to run**
That's **your own control plane** (`aksh-dogfood-app`) — preloop reading the same YAML, creating its own check run, and scheduling the job onto a smolvm microVM on `main`. preloop names check runs after the *job id* (`zizmor`, `rust`, `runner-light`), which is why its entries are bare names with no `workflow / job (event)` decoration.

## Why there are two

This is dogfooding, working as designed: preloop exists to replicate GitHub Actions, so it subscribes to the same `push`/`pull_request` events and executes the same workflows. GitHub Actions doesn't know that and keeps running them too. Every workflow therefore produces two check runs — one from each engine. The naming convention is the reliable way to tell them apart:

| | GitHub Actions | preloop |
|---|---|---|
| App | `github-actions` | `aksh-dogfood-app` |
| Name | `workflow / job (event)` | just `job` |
| Runs on | GitHub hosted runners | smolvm microVM on `main` |

You can see the split cleanly above: `rust`, `property-tests-*`, `runner-*`, `server-light` exist **only** as preloop checks (GitHub Actions isn't running those — presumably `runs-on: self-hosted`, so Actions has no runner for them), while `zizmor` is the one workflow both engines can run, hence the duplicate.

content.text:
Because it's pinned there deliberately — `/etc/preloop/preloop.env:5`:

```
PRELOOP_RUNNER_POOL_SIZE=1
PRELOOP_RUNNER_MEMORY_MIB=8192
```

That's a **warm pool of one**, so steady state is one runner slot plus the frozen golden. Nothing is broken.

## What the default would have been

With the env var unset, `host_runner_pool_size(RUNNER_CPUS=4)` computes:

$$\text{by\_cpu} = \left\lfloor \frac{6\ \text{cores}}{4} \right\rfloor = 1 \qquad \text{by\_memory} = \frac{23297}{8 \times 400} \approx 7$$

$$\text{target} = \min(1 \times 2,\ 7,\ 8) = 2$$

So the default *would* be 2, and `=1` halves it. But that default assumes the 4096 MiB stock runner; you've overridden runners to **8192 MiB**, which the formula's `IDLE_RUNNER_MIB = 400` heuristic doesn't account for.

## Why 1 is the right call here

Every VM is 4 vCPU / 8 GiB, and the host has 6 cores / 23 GB:

```
preloop-runner-golden-3577f5d5a384   cpus=4  mem=8192MiB  frozen    ← fork base, holds RAM
preloop-runner-0-6                   cpus=4  mem=8192MiB  running
```

Two concurrent clones plus the frozen golden is nominally 24 GB against 23.3 GB total — and right now you're at 15.3 GB used with **7.9 GB available**. A second 8 GB runner wouldn't fit without swapping. CPU is just as tight: one runner already claims 4 of 6 cores, so two would oversubscribe.

CoW forking means clones share pages with the golden initially, so real usage is below nominal — but it grows as jobs dirty pages, and this is the box that runs your control plane too.

## You did see two earlier

Correct, and that's expected: during handoff the pool replenishes the next slot while the current job finishes, so two clones coexist transiently (`0-17`/`0-18`, `0-21`/`0-22`). Steady state returns to one.

## The tradeoff

Pool size 1 means **strictly serial CI** — one job at a time, which is exactly why today's backlog drained so slowly and why `rust` (a full `cargo test --workspace`) blocks everything behind it for ~30 minutes. If you want parallelism, the lever isn't the pool count alone; you'd need to drop `PRELOOP_RUNNER_MEMORY_MIB` (say 8192 → 5120) so two runners fit in RAM, and accept 8 vCPU oversubscribed on 6 cores. content.text:
Your arithmetic misses one term, but the real blocker is something else entirely — and it's worse than the arithmetic.

## The missing term

It's not 2 × 8 GB. The **frozen golden also holds a VM**, because it's the CoW fork base every clone is cut from:

$$\underbrace{8}_{\text{golden}} + \underbrace{8 + 8}_{\text{2 clones}} = 24\ \text{GB nominal} \;>\; 23.3\ \text{GB total}$$

## But nominal isn't what's consumed — you're right about that

Measured just now:

```
preloop-runner-golden-3577f5d5a384  frozen   rss=0.30 GiB   (nominal 8192 MiB)
preloop-runner-0-6                  running  rss=2.03 GiB   (nominal 8192 MiB)
shared: 10005 MiB   ← memfd guest RAM shared between golden and clone
```

8192 MiB is a **ceiling, not a reservation**. CoW + lazy allocation means a clone starts near-free and grows only as it dirties pages. So two clones would not cost 16 GB up front. Your instinct is sound.

## The actual blocker

```
              total    used    free   shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          23297   15323    5568    10005       12806        7973
Swap:          8191    8088     103        ←  98.7% FULL
```

**Swap is exhausted with a single runner.** The box has already pushed 8 GB out, and the preloop cgroup alone is at 13.4 GiB. There is no headroom for a second VM's growth — and clone RSS grows exactly when it hurts, during `cargo test --workspace`, which is the job that pins a runner for ~30 minutes.

This also reframes today's failures: the cold-boot path died with **exit 137 = SIGKILL**, with no host OOM-killer entry but swap in this state. Memory pressure is a live suspect I dismissed too quickly at the time.

## So: not as-is

Adding a second 8 GB-ceiling slot on a box that's already swap-saturated is how you turn "slow CI" into "randomly killed jobs" — the failure mode that's hardest to debug, and we've already burned a day on one of those.

If you want parallelism, change the ceiling too, not just the count:

```
PRELOOP_RUNNER_POOL_SIZE=2
PRELOOP_RUNNER_MEMORY_MIB=5120     # 2 clones + golden ≈ 15 GB ceiling
```

Even then CPU is oversubscribed — 2 × 4 vCPU on 6 cores — so two parallel `cargo test`s may each run slower than one after another, netting no throughput gain.

Before changing anything I'd measure the peak: watch `MemoryCurrent` and swap through one full `rust` job. If a single clone peaks near 8 GB, a second slot can't fit at any ceiling that still builds Rust, and the honest answer is that this host needs more RAM rather than more slots. That's a 30-minute observation, and I'd rather have the number than guess — happy to run it.

That reframes it — I was too alarmist. The measurements say the box is **not** under pressure:

```
si/so:            0  0   (after the first sample; no active swapping)
memory pressure:  some avg10=0.00  avg60=0.00  avg300=0.00
free:             5.5 GB + 13.1 GB cache
top consumers:    preloop 2.17 GiB, libkrun(clone) 2.03 GiB, libkrun(golden) 0.30 GiB
```

The 8 GB of swap is **stale residue** from today's churn — pages parked and never touched again, not a working set. PSI at `0.00` across all windows is the definitive signal: nothing has stalled on memory recently. And the real consumers are modest — preloop itself is 2.17 GiB, not the 13.4 GiB the cgroup reported (that figure counts page cache).

## So does 2 × 6 GB work?

Nominal ceilings: $6 + 6 + 6 = 18$ GB against 23.3 GB, leaving ~5 GB for host + preloop's ~2.2 GB. That fits, and since ceilings are lazy, real usage would sit well under it.

The risk moves **inside the guest**, not on the host. A runner with 4 vCPU runs 4 parallel `rustc` processes during `cargo test --workspace`; heavy crates can hit 1–3 GB each. 8 GB currently absorbs that. At 6 GB you'd be trading a host-level constraint for in-guest OOM during exactly the job that matters most — and an OOM-killed `rustc` surfaces as a confusing job failure, not a clean "out of memory" verdict.

## What I'd do

Two variables are changing at once (slots 1→2, ceiling 8→6). Split them:

1. **Measure the peak first.** Watch one full `rust` job and record the clone's peak RSS. If it peaks at ~3 GB, 6 GB is comfortable and 2 slots are clearly safe. If it peaks near 7 GB, 6 GB will fail and you have your answer without an outage.
2. **Then change one thing.** If the peak allows it, go `PRELOOP_RUNNER_POOL_SIZE=2` and keep `8192` — 8+8+8=24 GB nominal exceeds RAM, but ceilings are lazy and PSI shows real headroom. That's the smaller change, and it leaves per-job memory untouched.

CPU remains the honest cap either way: 2 × 4 vCPU on 6 cores means two parallel `cargo test`s will contend, so expect better *latency for short jobs* (zizmor, runner-light stop queueing behind `rust`) rather than more total throughput.

Want me to run the measurement? It's passive — sample the clone's RSS every 10 s through the next `rust` job and report the peak. No config changes, no restart, and then the decision is arithmetic instead of judgment.

## Why still no PRs

```

Last Job Run: 1 hour ago ✅ it has actually run
PRs / issues created:    none
Dependency Updates (Renovate): Silent   ← this
```

**Silent mode** is exactly what it sounds like: Renovate scans, resolves updates, and reports them to the Mend dashboard, but creates **no PRs and no Dependency Dashboard issue**. That's Mend's default for new Community (Free) installs — it's opt-in before it starts writing to your repo. It perfectly explains the contradiction: a job ran an hour ago, yet GitHub shows nothing.

So nothing is misconfigured in `renovate.json`. Your customManagers are fine; they're just running with the pen taken away.

## Fix

In that same panel: **Default Engine Settings → Dependency Updates (Renovate) → change `Silent` to enabled**. It's org-wide, and can also be set per-repo from the repo row if you'd rather switch on `preloop` alone first — which I'd suggest, given 25 repos are onboarded and flipping org-wide could open PRs across all of them at once.

Once flipped, expect on the next job run:
- a **Dependency Dashboard** issue
- `actions/runner` 2.336.0 → **v2.337.0**, labeled `protocol-sync` (the runner-watch tripwire, no auto-merge)
- `smolvm` 1.8.2 → **v1.13.1**, which your config marks `automerge: true`

## Before you flip it

That smolvm auto-merge is still the sharp edge I flagged earlier, and it's now imminent rather than theoretical:

- Your own config comment says the verify gate is **inert** until a `[self-hosted, macOS, ARM64, smolvm-host]` runner exists and `SMOLVM_VERIFY_HOST_WORKSPACE` is set. Auto-merging a 1.8.2 → 1.13.1 jump through an inert gate lands five minors unreviewed.
- `smolvm_golden_version` tracks **upstream** `smol-machines/smolvm`. Prod now runs 1.13.1 built from *your fork* with the clock patch. A bump to upstream v1.13.1 points the golden at a build **without** it — silently reintroducing today's outage.

I'd set `automerge: false` for smolvm (or repoint that pin at your fork) in the same sitting as flipping Silent off. Want me to open that config PR? It's a one-line change, and per your rules I'll leave the actual version-bump PRs to Renovate.

content.text:
CI didn't fail on your code — **the host ran out of memory and the kernel killed the VM.**

## The chain

```
22:23:55  cc1 (gcc) OOM-killed  — inside actions.runner.…aksh-golden-x64.service
22:24:04  libkrun VM OOM-killed — anon-rss 8,073,908 kB  (the full 8 GiB runner)
22:24:14  preloop.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'
22:24:30  "failed job claims orphaned by a control-plane restart count=1"
```

`global_oom, constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE` — that's a **host-wide** OOM, not a cgroup limit (`MemoryMax=infinity`). The kernel picked the biggest anonymous consumer, which was the 8 GiB runner VM. Killing it took the control plane down with it, orphaning the in-flight job. That's why `rust` and `server-light` show `failure` on `12721ff3`, and why three others are still `queued`.

It happened **twice** (22:06 and 22:24), and `MemoryPeak` for the unit is **18.1 GiB** on a 23.3 GiB box.

## What pushed it over

The release fired several heavy workflows at once, and the golden ones run on **self-hosted** runners — i.e. this same box:

```
Build & Publish Golden MicroVM Artifact   failure     ← the one I flagged as unnecessary
Build Linux runner bundle (x2)            success
Build Linux aarch64 / x86_64 release      in_progress
release-golden                            queued
```

So the golden build (compiling inside `aksh-golden-x64`, hence `cc1`) was running *concurrently* with preloop's own `rust` job in an 8 GiB microVM. Two heavy compiles, one 23 GiB host.

Note the golden build is exactly the work I said was unnecessary — bake content hasn't changed since v0.31.1, and the `skip-golden` marker never reached the release body. **The wasted golden rebuild is what OOM-killed your CI.**

## This also settles the pool-size question

Earlier I measured PSI `0.00` and no swap traffic and said there was headroom. That was measured **idle**. Under real load the unit peaks at 18.1 GiB. So:

> **No — you cannot run 2 × 6 GB VMs.** The box can't reliably sustain *one* 8 GiB runner during a Rust build when anything else is compiling.

My earlier "there's headroom" read was wrong because it sampled the wrong moment; this is the measurement I proposed taking, and the answer arrived the hard way.

## What I'd do, in order

1. **Cancel the queued `release-golden` run** — it's unnecessary for this release and it's the thing that blew up memory.
2. **Fix the guard** so golden rebuilds are opt-in (`preloop:build-golden`) rather than relying on a changelog marker cargo-dist discards.
3. **Re-run the failed checks** on `12721ff3` once the box is quiet — the code is almost certainly fine, since the identical tree passed `just test-ci` locally.
4. Longer term: keep golden builds off the same host as the CI pool, or cap the runner VM so a host OOM can't take the control plane with it.

Source-level confirmation of the limitation: the dispatch adapter hardcodes `sha: None`, so **any** submitted `workflow_dispatch` run checks out `0000…0000`. That path can't validate a checkout-based workflow — the webhook-driven PR run can, which is how `main` went green.

**Base:** `main` ← **Head:** `fix/golden-release-optin`

arguments.content:
{
  "op": "pr_create",
  "repo": "preloopdev/preloop",
  "title": "fix(ci): make release golden rebuilds opt-in",
  "head": "fix/golden-release-optin",
  "base": "main",
  "draft": true,
  "body": "## Problem

The `skip-golden` guard never worked. `release.yml` is cargo-dist generated and **owns the release body** — it writes install/download instructions from scratch — so the `<!-- preloop:skip-golden -->` marker placed in `CHANGELOG.md` never reached `github.event.release.body`. The guard

```yaml
if: ... || (github.event_name == 'release' && !contains(github.event.release.body, '<!-- preloop:skip-golden -->'))
```

was therefore always true, and **every** release rebuilt the golden — including releases whose bake content (packages, install script) had not changed.

Verified on v0.32.0: the marker was in the changelog section, and the published release body still reported `skip-golden marker present: false`.

## Why it matters

`build-and-publish-golden` runs on `[self-hosted, Linux, X64]` — the same host as the runner pool. On v0.32.0 it compiled (`cc1`) alongside a `cargo test --workspace` job and triggered a host-wide OOM:

```
oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE ... global_oom, task=cc1
Out of memory: Killed process (libkrun VM) anon-rss:8073908kB
preloop.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'
```

That killed the 8 GiB runner VM and took `preloop.service` with it, orphaning the in-flight job (`failed job claims orphaned by a control-plane restart`). `rust` and `server-light` failed on a release commit whose tree had passed `just test-ci` locally. It happened twice (22:06 and 22:24); unit `MemoryPeak` hit 18.1 GiB on a 23.3 GiB host.

## Change

Invert both guards to opt **in** on `<!-- preloop:build-golden -->`, so a release no longer rebuilds the golden unless explicitly asked. Deliberate golden builds keep running via `workflow_dispatch`, which is how they have actually been produced in practice (the last successful golden build was a manual dispatch on Aug 24).

A comment records why, so the broken opt-out marker is not reintroduced.

## Validation

YAML parses; `zizmor` reports `No findings to report` on the changed file — the same linter CI runs.

Note: `preloop-runner-client submit --event workflow_dispatch` cannot validate this repo's `ci.yml`, because `events/workflow_dispatch.rs` sets `sha: None`, so `actions/checkout` fetches `0000000000000000000000000000000000000000` and fails with `upload-pack: not our ref`. Worth fixing separately — it makes the submit-before-push path unusable for any checkout-based workflow.
"
}

Not your code — queue contention on a single-slot pool. The pool is busy with **PR #190** (`9f75fe1c`, memory-hardening), and with `pool_size=1` every `rust` job is ~25–30 min serialized. Three other non-draft PRs (#190, #188, #111) are ahead of my draft.

The release fired `release-golden` on `[self-hosted, Linux, X64]` — the same host as the runner pool — which compiled alongside `cargo test --workspace` and caused a **host-wide OOM** (`global_oom, CONSTRAINT_NONE`) that killed the 8 GiB runner VM and `preloop.service`. `rust`/`server-light` on `12721ff3` are collateral, not real failures. That commit's tree passed `just test-ci` locally, and its jobs are now checking out cleanly (`fetch +12721ff3…` succeeded at 23:24/23:28).

PR #193 is precisely what stops that recurring.

I don't think grinding the queue further tonight is wise — the host has OOM-killed the control plane four times and is at 210 MB free right now. Options:

1. **Merge #193 on the strength of what's verified** — it's a workflow-guard change; YAML + zizmor are the checks that actually cover it, and it removes a known outage cause before the next release.

content.text:
## First, correct the premise

0.32.0 shipped **no observability**. I checked:

- `git show origin/main:CHANGELOG.md` §0.32.0 — cancellation process-group fix, smolvm version pinning, golden download timeout/progress, the GitHub App webhook warning. Nothing telemetry-related.
- No `opentelemetry`, `opentelemetry-otlp`, `tracing-opentelemetry`, `prometheus`, or `metrics-exporter-*` in any `Cargo.toml`.
- No `/stats`, no `/metrics` route. Only `/healthz` (`routes.rs:256`).
- Zero matches for `otlp|opentelemetry|openobserve` across `crates/**/*.rs`.

So this isn't "deploy OpenObserve and point it at preloop." **Nothing emits telemetry yet.** The bulk of the work is in preloop, not in ops.

## What prod looks like today

```
aksh.preloop.dev → cloudflared tunnel 16cc97ea → http://127.0.0.1:9090 (preloop)
                   single ingress rule, then http_status:404
```
No nginx/caddy/traefik. Docker active, zero containers. `tracing_subscriber::fmt()` at `main.rs:78` logs to stdout → journald, and that's the entire telemetry story.

## The process, in dependency order

**Phase 1 — instrument preloop (code, the real work).** Add an OTLP layer alongside the existing fmt layer in `main.rs:78`; it's additive:

```rust
tracing_subscriber::registry()
    .with(tracing_subscriber::fmt::layer())
    .with(EnvFilter::from_default_env())
    .with(tracing_opentelemetry::layer().with_tracer(otlp_tracer));  // new
```

Then decide what's actually worth emitting. Based on tonight, the metrics that would have caught everything: queue depth, time-to-provision, pool VM count/state, golden bake attempts + `stop agent` failures, job duration by name, and **host/VM RSS**.

**Phase 2 — host OpenObserve.** Single container, loopback-bound:

```bash
docker run -d --name openobserve --restart unless-stopped \
  --memory 2g --memory-swap 2g \
  -p 127.0.0.1:5080:5080 \
  -v /var/lib/openobserve:/data \
  -e ZO_DATA_DIR=/data -e ZO_TELEMETRY=false \
  -e ZO_ROOT_USER_EMAIL=... -e ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD=... \
  openobserve/openobserve:latest
```
5080 = UI + OTLP/HTTP ingest, 5081 = OTLP/gRPC. `ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD` is read **only on first boot**. Set retention (`ZO_COMPACT_DATA_RETENTION_DAYS`) up front.

**Phase 3 — expose it authed.** Add a second cloudflared ingress. Path-based `/stats` on the existing hostname works but needs `ZO_BASE_URI=/stats`:

```yaml
ingress:
  - hostname: aksh.preloop.dev
    path: ^/stats
    service: http://127.0.0.1:5080
  - hostname: aksh.preloop.dev
    service: http://127.0.0.1:9090
  - service: http_status:404
```

For auth, put **Cloudflare Access** in front of that path — you're already on a CF tunnel, so it's SSO with zero code, and it's strictly better than exposing OpenObserve's single root login to the internet. Don't try to proxy it through preloop's bearer auth; that means writing a reverse proxy into the server for no gain.

## Pushback on the host

That box OOM-killed the control plane **four times tonight** at 23.3 GB with pool=1, and killed two CI jobs. Adding a always-on ingest+compaction daemon to the same machine is how you turn tonight's incident into a recurring one. Either cap it hard (as above) and cap the runner VM, or — better — run OpenObserve somewhere else and ship OTLP to it. The one thing you must not do is let the telemetry stack compete with the thing it's meant to observe.

## The fork worth deciding before any of this

"Real-time info at /stats" splits into two different products, and OpenObserve is only right for one:

I owe you a straight correction: **you were right, I was wrong twice.**

The observability crate landed in **#187** (`081e7877`, 08-27) and `git tag --contains` confirms it **is in v0.32.0**. My "0.32.0 shipped no observability" came from reading only the `### Fixed`/`### Changed` prose and grepping a stale branch. Bad process on my part.

Here's the real state:

| | |
|---|---|
| Crate | `preloop-observability` — OTLP traces/logs/metrics, Prometheus, status snapshot, VM telemetry |
| Endpoints | `/metrics` + `/api/v1/status`, already behind `require_native_bearer` |
| Config | Standard `OTEL_*` env vars — **no code needed to point at OpenObserve** |
| **Prod** | **still 0.31.1** — binary has zero `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` symbols, `/metrics` → 404 |

Endpoint semantics are already correct for OpenObserve: the generic var gets `/v1/traces` appended (signal-specific ones are used as-is, explicitly to avoid `/v1/traces/v1/traces`). So `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:5080/api/default` resolves exactly to OpenObserve's ingest paths.

So the process is **four ops steps, zero code**:

1. Upgrade prod 0.31.1 → 0.32.0 (this alone lights up `/metrics` and `/api/v1/status`)
2. Run OpenObserve
3. Set `OTEL_*` in `/etc/preloop/preloop.env`, restart preloop
4. Expose `/stats` via cloudflared + Cloudflare Access

Starting with the additive, zero-risk part — OpenObserve itself, capped so it can't repeat tonight:

`/stats` is live. Here's where things stand — including a second, bigger correction.

## I was wrong about the outage too

I told you the golden rebuild caused the OOM. The actual cause was sitting in every `free` output I looked at tonight, in the `shared` column:

**Pullfrog was leaking repo clones into `/tmp`, which is a `size=50%` tmpfs — i.e. RAM.**

```
tmpfs  12G  12G  0  100% /tmp      ← 58 × /tmp/pullfrog-XXXXXX @ 469 MB
```

12 GB of your 23.3 GB was permanently consumed, leaving ~11 GB for an 8 GB runner VM plus `cargo`/`cc1`/`npm`. That's why the box OOM-killed the control plane four times. `pullfrog.yml` runs `on: pull_request [opened, synchronize, reopened]` + `issue_comment` on `self-hosted`, and the action never cleans up — ~58 clones accumulated since 10:23 today. The golden build didn't create the condition; it just landed on a box that was already out of headroom.

Reclaimed, with zero processes holding handles:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `/tmp` | 12 G (100%) | **164 M (2%)** |
| available RAM | 7.2 G | **10.9 G** |

Guards installed: `pullfrog-tmp-reap.timer` (hourly, reaps `pullfrog-*` older than 2h, active) and `OOMScoreAdjust=-500` on `preloop.service` so builds die before the control plane does.

## Observability — you were right

`preloop-observability` landed in **#187** (`081e7877`) and `git tag --contains` puts it in **v0.32.0**. My "no observability" claim came from grepping my stale feature branch and skimming only the changelog's `Fixed`/`Changed` prose. It uses standard `OTEL_*` env vars, so **no code was needed** — this was pure ops.

## Live now

```
https://aksh.preloop.dev/stats/web/   → 200
https://aksh.preloop.dev/healthz      → 200   (preloop untouched)
```

- OpenObserve container: 125 MB RSS, hard cap 1.46 GiB / 1.5 CPU, 14-day retention, loopback-bound
- OTLP ingest verified end-to-end — records queried back out; unauthed → **401**
- cloudflared: `path: ^/stats` → `:5080`, everything else → `:9090`; `ingress validate` OK, rule-match tested both ways
- `ZO_BASE_URI=/stats` (cloudflared can't strip prefixes), ingest endpoint adjusted to `/stats/api/default` to match
